newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - EMU technology changes demand action.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EMU technology changes demand action.

text.p: LONDON, Oct 16 Reuter - Major adaptations to computer systems ahead of European Economic and Monetary Union will hit a brick wall unless industry standards for the transformation are set by the end of 1996, industry analysts say.
A senior manager, involved in EMU planning at a major British bank said it was difficult for individual banks to progress beyond the planning stage.

"Put it this way, we're not ready to start writing code tomorrow," he said. "The continentals are in the same position. There are no design details available and the state of readiness ranges from black alert to red alert."

Although EMU may seem a long way off, with a planned start date of January 1999, the British Bankers Association (BBA) said it estimates necessary information technology changes will take about three years.
That means any bank intending to be ready at the start-date of EMU, known informally as E-Day, should already have its plans in hand.
MASSIVE SCALE OF CHANGES
A recent test-run of an EMU scenario on software at a French bank revealed that of one million programming lines, 8,000 were directly affected and a further 15,000 were indirectly affected.
But despite the massive scale of required changes, plans at British banks are not as well developed as in Germany and France where political will to be at the forefront of EMU is strong.
In Germany, commercial banks made an agreement earlier this year with the central bank, the Bundesbank, to operate their systems in both euros and marks from the beginning of 1999.
"German banks have made exemplary progress," said Dr Stefan Collignon, director of research at the Association for the Monetary Union of Europe in France.
He also pointed out that the Italian Banking Association was considering starting a training course on the Euro for all of the country's 330,000 banking employees.
BOND TRADES PROBLEMATIC
But what industry sources say they lack are agreements on the nuts-and-bolts rules on which existing bond markets rely.

Problems for bond-trading systems include how many days there will be in a bond year (whether the new euro-denominated bonds will use the British 365 days or the German 360 days), and which rounding algorithms will be used to convert historic values into euro debt issues.

The BBA and Britain's Association for Payment Clearing Services (APACS) had previously estimated a cost of 1.0 billion pounds ($1.58 billion) for British wholesale and retail banks to make required changes, but they now say these could be doubled.

Unlike the relatively simple task of adding a new bond from an existing country to current computer systems, euro instruments will come into existence over a three year period at a time when individual countries' bonds are still trading.
During this so-called "migration period', bonds could be issued in both the euro and the domestic currency and settled by investors who do not necessarily have euro accounts.

"It's now generally expected that the technological costs of a phased in introduction of EMU will be higher than the "big bang' method," said Roger Brown, director of statistics and economics at the BBA.
Banks will also be required to keep records of all their transactions in "dual entry' system during the migration period, effectively doubling the capacity needed for data storage.

"Trades will have to be done at a time when people are at different stages of developing their IT and using equivalent currencies," said John Gubert, chairman of the LIBA and also a senior manager at HSBC Holdings. "The core standard information -- the things banks don't need to check, things we rely on -- will change."
BRITISH POSITION AWKWARD

Analysts said the wait-and-see attitude of British policy makers to Britain's entry into EMU means British banks are in a more awkward position, being forced to take a gamble on whether or not to spend money on changes.

Paying out large amounts of money on technology could leave banks with a costly white elephant if Britain decided not to join. On the other hand, failure to start now could result in an unseemly and even more expensive scramble if Britain does decide to go in.
Collignon also warned that those institutions waiting too long would not find the necessary manpower.

"Many organisations have taken the view that they have got to get prepared come what may," said Stewart MacKinnon, head of European affairs at APACS. "The investment decisions may have to be taken before we have the political decision."
LIBA's Gubert said the British banking industry will have to get ready for EMU anyway, in order to deal internationally with those countries that are members.

A further cost involved comes from recruiting computer experts to deal with the situation. EMU must be implemented at a time when companies are working to resolve the difficulties of reprogramming older computer systems, so-called "legacy systems' to recognise the year 2000.

Because older computers use only the last two digits of a year, they will interpret the year 2000 as the year 1900. That could result in electronically held records being deleted and automated cash transfers ceasing to work.

The British government-sponsored group Taskforce 2000 has estimated that as much as 80 percent of computers will be affected, and that there may not be enough computer experts to tackle both EMU and the year 2000 at the same time.
But the senior manager at a British bank said most banks were already expanding their existing in-house IT staff.

Alec Nacamuli, head of payments at computer-giant IBM's consultancy group based in London said core European countries were relatively well advanced in planning, but would not start implementing changes until early next year.

"Most banks realise they must also review their strategic and business planning to face the new competitive Euro-landscape," he said. "They don't always have the necessary resources to do everything in-house and are calling on external consultancies for help."
Since many systems are already running at or near full capacity, banks would be likely to outsource testing of new software and platforms.
He said many financial institutions were taking this opportunity to upgrade and revamp all their computer systems.
But for many banks E-day is January 1997, when they must start the countdown to the technological changeover.

"The project becomes higher and higher risk the longer the uncertainties continue and we think the risk will be unpalatable by the end of the year," said LIBA's Gubert. "There is no time now to just raise the issues - we've got to come up with proposals."
